Artificial Intelligence for Cardiac Ischemia Detection: A Review of Biosensor, Biomarker, and Imaging Applications.
desc: [Sensors (Basel, Switzerland)] Ischemic heart disease is the leading cause of global mortality, yet accurate and timely detection remains constrained by incomplete signal capture, noise, operator dependence, and imperfect reference standards. Artificial intelligence (AI) may enhance cardiovascular sensing by extracting latent diagnostic information from routinely acquired signals. This narrative review examines AI-enabled approaches to ischemia detection across three sensing modalities: the electrocardiogram as a bioelectric sensor, cardiac troponin as a biochemical marker, and cardiac imaging technologies (echocardiography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance, and nuclear imaging) as structural and functional sensors. For each modality, we evaluate the sensing pipeline, the reference standards, the endpoint actually measured (from acute coronary occlusion to functional ischemia), and reported performance metrics, separating diagnostic accuracy from effects on clinical workflow, patient outcomes, and cost. We also discuss emerging directions, including foundation models and multimodal fusion, together with translational challenges such as limited prospective validation, regulatory hurdles, and uncertain cost-effectiveness. Most evidence comes from retrospective, frequently single-center studies of diagnostic performance; few studies have measured effects on workflow, and fewer still on patient outcomes or cost. Routine clinical adoption will require prospective multicenter trials, standardized performance benchmarks, and evidence of clinical and economic benefit.

title: PathCowork: Learning from real-world pathology practice to build AI copilots
desc: Medical AI learns from the answers doctors record, but rarely from how they interpret the evidence to reach them. Here we introduce PathCowork, a framework that turns pathologists' narrated examinations into supervision for visual grounding and procedures that guide diagnostic AI agents. Synchronized gaze, narration and navigation link visual findings to the process of interpreting them. Across 48 sessions from 16 pathologists, the platform captured 1,028 minutes of slide review. Using these data, we trained PathCowork-1T for server deployment and PathCowork-27B for local deployment, with improved visual grounding. Across five organ-specific evaluations, agents combining this grounding with recorded diagnostic procedures achieved primary task scores averaging 17.9 and 24.1 percentage points higher than Claude Code and Codex, respectively, with shorter processing times and lower inference costs. Compared to the state-of-the-art multiple-instance learning AIs, the PathCowork agent-proposed regions achieved higher prostate-grading scores with limited slide labels. PathCowork can also help construct pathology AI benchmarks where questions derived from the recordings identified difficulties in recognizing viewing context and rejecting inapplicable premises. In summary, PathCowork proposes a new paradigm to scale up the data collection and train pathology AI through transparent reasoning from diagnostic sessions, opening a path towards systems that learn directly from routine clinical practice.

title: A narrative review of methods for estimating blood pressure waveforms from photoplethysmography.
source: PubMed · Journal of clinical monitoring and computing
desc: [Journal of clinical monitoring and computing] Accurate, continuous blood pressure (BP) monitoring is important for preventing, diagnosing, and managing cardiovascular disease. Estimating the full arterial BP waveform can provide more clinical information than cuff-based measurements that report only systolic and diastolic BP. This review summarizes recent progress in predicting arterial BP waveforms from photoplethysmography (PPG) and identifies the main methodological gaps that limit clinical translation. We reviewed research published since 2021 on PPG-based BP waveform estimation. We organized the literature around core pipeline elements, including open-source datasets, preprocessing and quality control, model architectures, and validation practices. We also surveyed commercially available technologies that measure BP waveform. Data cleaning approaches can be grouped into three main categories: (1) template-based pulsation comparison, (2) feature extraction paired with classical machine learning, and (3) neural network-based quality assessment. For waveform prediction, recent work is dominated by deep learning, particularly U-Net-based architectures, autoencoder families, and attention-based models. Progress in PPG-based BP waveform prediction is rapid, but comparability and reproducibility remain major barriers. Benchmark datasets with consistent acquisition protocols, transparent preprocessing, and standardized validation criteria are needed to support fair comparison.

title: Conformal Annotation with Randomized Expert Review: Application to Online Cell-Type Labeling
desc: Artificial intelligence (AI) models can accelerate cell-type annotation in digital pathology, but safely scaling their use requires determining, with error control, which model-generated labels can be accepted without expert review. This is challenging in evolving workflows because cell morphology and type composition may change across tissue regions and slides, making one-time calibration unreliable. We propose Conformal Annotation with Randomized Expert review under Distribution shift (CARED), a distribution-free framework that leverages randomized expert audit to achieve long-run error control for AI-assisted annotation under distribution shift. For each incoming batch, CARED uniformly selects a subset of cases for expert review and uses the acquired labels to calibrate later decisions. Among unreviewed cases, CARED determines a subset of them to safely skip expert labeling, while suggesting candidate labels for the others for downstream resolution. We prove that this workflow provides long-run control of cumulative error over both the full stream and the cells outside of the audit sample, without stationarity or exchangeability assumptions. We further enhance the framework by introducing class-conditional guarantees to ensure error control within important but rare cell types, together with a utility module to target more automatic resolutions, smaller candidate sets, and greater biological coherence, without compromising validity. Experiments on pancreas, lung, and ovary annotation streams, together with a stream constructed from real expert annotations, show that CARED controls the cumulative errors while a substantial fraction of cells (up to 70%) bypass expert review.

title: Adaptive Precision Nutrition: Integrating Dynamic Phenotyping, Multi-Omics, Artificial Intelligence, and the Allostatic Viability Principle.
desc: [Nutrients] Precision nutrition increasingly combines functional foods, multi-omics, digital phenotyping, and artificial intelligence, yet the incremental decision value of additional data layers remains uncertain. This critical narrative review and hypothesis-generating conceptual proposal examines evidence on personalized nutrition, dynamic response phenotyping, functional-food heterogeneity, multi-omics integration, and AI-supported decisions. Personalized advice can improve dietary behavior and selected cardiometabolic outcomes, whereas the additional clinical benefit attributable specifically to elaborate molecular profiling has been inconsistent. Dynamic challenge studies suggest that response amplitude, timing, coordination, recovery, and conditional repeatability may provide information beyond static profiles, but reproducibility is required before these features can be treated as person-specific traits. The Allostatic Viability Principle (AVP) is proposed as a conceptual physiological and decision framework rather than a validated predictor or biomarker. Its intended contribution is to organize existing approaches around viable, context-appropriate regulation, proportional use of additional measurements, explicit uncertainty, an outcome hierarchy that does not equate molecular change with health benefit, and a response-and-revision loop. Whether this organization improves decisions or outcomes beyond high-quality conventional or adaptive personalized nutrition remains an empirical question. The framework is therefore presented as a testable structure for determining when additional individual-level information is reproducible, relevant, and sufficiently decision changing to justify use.

title: Uncertainty-aware Coarse-to-Fine Main Pancreatic Duct Segmentation for Width Measurement in 3D MRCP
desc: Assessment of the main pancreatic duct (MPD) from volumetric magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) scans is an essential task for ductal dilatation diagnosis and pancreatic cancer analysis. However, manual assessment is affected by reader variability in which automated analysis may assist. Nevertheless, fully automated and uncertainty-aware MPD analysis from volumetric MRCP remains underexplored area of research. In this study, we propose an automatic and uncertainty-aware deep learning-based pipeline for MPD segmentation and maximum-width analysis from MRCP scans. A coarse localisation model first identifies the ductal region-of-interest, followed by a fine model that segments the MPD within the region. The dataset consists of 256 MPD-segmented MRCP scans from 69 patients. A randomly selected holdout test subset of 14 patients with 55 MRCP volumes was used for evaluation. We employed a five-model cross-validation ensemble for improved performance and uncertainty estimation. The best MPD segmentation performance was 0.634 DSC, 0.744 precision, and 0.593 recall. The mean absolute error for maximum MPD width prediction was 0.355~mm and dilated MPD ($\geq 5$~mm) was detected with 75.0\% sensitivity and 74.4\% specificity. These novel results suggest that automated MPD segmentation can be used to aid MRCP-based duct measurements.

title: The Advent of Big Data and Machine Learning in Ophthalmology: The 2026 Cogan Lecture.
desc: [Investigative ophthalmology & visual science] The major objective of this lecture is to summarize the evolution of computational ophthalmology over the past 2 decades through the scientific advances that have transformed ophthalmic research. Topics include the emergence of computational ophthalmology, the role of big data in scientific discovery, the application of machine learning to ophthalmic imaging, and the development of artificial intelligence (AI)-ready data ecosystems. The lecture concludes by exploring the next frontier in computational ophthalmology, highlighting foundation models and agentic AI as emerging approaches with the potential to accelerate scientific discovery, and improve clinical care are discussed. This article is based on the 2026 Cogan Award Lecture presented by Aaron Y. Lee, MD, MSCI, and Cecilia S. Lee, MD, MS, at ARVO 2026.

title: BRACHIO: Broad Representations Across Centres for Head-and-neck Imaging Oncology (HECKTOR 2026)
desc: The HECKTOR 2026 challenge benchmarks machine learning for head and neck cancer, where teams delineate primary and nodal tumour volumes, perform TN staging, and predict recurrence-free survival (RFS). This report describes the submissions for the HECKTOR challenge of team nucli. As the three tasks span both dense and global information from multicentric PET/CT scans, we utilise self-supervised pre-trained encoders, training a 2D DINOv2 encoder (PET-DINOv2-MIPs) on HECKTOR 2026's PET scans. Our final test submission ensembles a DynUNet trained from scratch with a SwinUNETR whose Swin trunk was initialised from a SimMIM-pre-trained checkpoint for segmentation, reaching a mean Dice of 0.5409. For TN staging, GTVp/GTVn geometric features from the segmentation masks are fit to stage probabilities by logistic regression (LR) and fused with PET-DINOv2-MIPs deep features (PCA + LR) via a second-level LR, reaching balanced accuracies of 0.3962 (T-stage) and 0.6432 (N-stage). For the RFS prognosis task, we fine-tune the last two blocks of the PET-DINOv2-MIPs ViT-S encoder jointly with an MLP head under a CoxPH loss, concatenating clinical covariates with the imaging features, reaching a test Harrell's C-index of 0.6577 and a weighted challenge score of 0.5802. The prognosis result is comparable to the best entry of the previous edition and consistent with our internal cross-validation, while our segmentation result is well below it and limits the staging results that depend on it.

title: Redesigning residency training with artificial intelligence: Implications for efficiency, quality, and workforce capacity.
source: PubMed · Journal of applied clinical medical physics
desc: [Journal of applied clinical medical physics] Workforce shortages and increasing clinical demands in Radiation Oncology and Medical Physics present challenges for maintaining high-quality residency training. This work presents a conceptual framework to evaluate the potential role of artificial intelligence (AI) in improving efficiency, scalability, and quality of residency education. Current teaching and learning modalities were categorized, and their relative contributions to training were estimated. Potential AI applications were mapped to these modalities, and the proportion of training that could be supported by AI was assessed. A simple conceptual model incorporating training time, AI-deliverable components (i.e., those potentially supported through direct interaction with AI systems), and dependence on direct human teaching was used to illustrate the potential impact on instructional effort. The potential effect of AI on educational quality was qualitatively evaluated, as well as limitations of AI for routine educational integration. AI applications were identified across multiple domains, including workflow-integrated feedback, simulation-based training, adaptive learning, and automated assessment. The largest potential impact was estimated in workflow-integrated, simulation-based, and self-directed learning environments. While reductions in direct human teaching effort were estimated to be modest, AI-enabled approaches were estimated to achieve substantial improvements in training quality, including increased feedback frequency, enhanced support for deliberate practice, and greater exposure to rare or high-risk scenarios. AI has the potential to enhance residency training by improving consistency, scalability, and educational quality. In the context of workforce constraints, the primary benefit of AI may be to augment training efficiency and reduce reliance on limited faculty resources while preserving the essential role of clinical experience.

title: Segment Anything Model Based Context Guided Mamba Unet for Medical Image Segmentation
desc: Medical image segmentation is crucial for clinical diagnosis and treatment planning, requiring both global contextual understanding and fine-grained structural precision. While the Segment Anything Model (SAM) demonstrates strong generalization capabilities, its direct application to medical images often lacks domain-specific adaptability. Meanwhile, State Space Models (SSMs)-based methods, such as Mamba, efficiently capture long-range dependencies but may struggle with preserving fine anatomical details. To address these challenges, we propose a segment anything model based context guided mamba unet, SAMBA-UNet, a novel framework that integrates SAM's context knowledge with Mamba's hierarchical feature learning to enhance both global representation and local detail refinement. Specifically, we introduce the Hierarchical Context Enhancement Module (HCEM), an attention-based fusion module that deeply incorporates the multi-level features of SAM and Mamba to improve detail perception and segmentation precision. Additionally, we employ LoRA and Adapter-based fine-tuning to adapt SAM to medical imaging tasks, further enhancing its domain-specific segmentation capability and robustness. We conducted a comprehensive study on several medical segmentation datasets, including Synapse, ISIC17, and ISIC18, evaluating our method across multiple metrics. Experimental results demonstrate that SAMBA-UNet achieves state-of-the-art performance, effectively balancing generalization, segmentation accuracy, and computational efficiency. Our code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Harnessing artificial intelligence to understand enzyme catalysis and discover new enzymes.
source: PubMed · Current opinion in structural biology
desc: [Current opinion in structural biology] Molecular simulations have been central to our understanding of how enzymes work, and the ongoing explosion of artificial intelligence/ML (AI/ML) approaches is greatly expanding the scope of problems that can be addressed using simulations. The speed of development of the field is tremendous, with the near-constant development of new approaches and successful applications. This review aims to give a higher-level overview of four key areas where AI/ML approaches are significantly transforming computational enzymology (both understanding and design), specifically (1) enzyme discovery and functional annotation, (2) kinetic parameter prediction, (3) understanding of protein dynamics and enzyme reaction mechanisms, and (4) decoding protein allostery. We also discuss some of the outstanding technical challenges in this research space, and efforts being made to overcome them.

title: Enhancing Atrial Fibrillation Detection Through Hyperparameter Optimization
desc: This study explores the role of hyperparameter optimization (HPO) in enhancing the detection of Atrial Fibrillation (AF) using both machine learning and deep learning models. We evaluated a range of standard classifiers - Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost classifiers, alongside deep learning architectures including Recurrent Neural Networks, Deep Neural Networks, and Siamese Neural Networks. To fine-tune these models, we applied four HPO methods: Genetic Algorithm, Hyperband, Optuna, and SMAC3. The experiments were conducted using inter-patient and intra- patient data splits to assess model generalization and robustness in the presence of class imbalance, which is reflective of real-world AF occurrence. Our results, based on PhysioNet electrocardiogram datasets, showed that the Hyperband-optimized XGBoost model outperformed all others, achieving a peak F1 score of 96.95%. These findings highlight the critical role of suitable HPO strategies in enhancing the accuracy and robustness of AF classification outcomes in clinical settings.

title: Exploring tinnitus-like central hyperactivity in a large language model-based computational analog of hearing loss.
desc: [Hearing research] Tinnitus is commonly associated with maladaptive neural plasticity following hearing loss. Although large language models (LLMs) share similarities with the human brain in language processing and representation, their potential for modeling tinnitus-related neural mechanisms remains limited. This study aimed to develop an LLM-based framework to investigate tinnitus-related maladaptive neural plasticity. An LLM was partitioned into eight independently trainable regions. An exploratory computational analogy of deafferentation-related changes associated with peripheral hearing loss was developed by applying token-specific high-frequency attenuation during training on a commonsense reasoning task. Region-specific contributions to tinnitus-like excess activity were quantified using region-wise plasticity ablation, selectively disabling plasticity in one region at a time. Representational relationships among regions were evaluated using centered kernel alignment. The computational deafferentation analog largely preserved task accuracy but showed increased activity. Region 1 was the only region with a net suppressive contribution to excess activity, whereas region 2 exhibited the largest positive contribution; regions 6 and 8 also contributed positively. Regions 1 and 2 remained representationally distinct across all conditions. Deafferentation tended to reduce region 1-region 2 similarity, whereas plasticity ablation in most regions, except for regions 6 and 8, tended to increase it. The proposed LLM-based framework captured network-level functional dissociations consistent with current theories of hearing loss-associated tinnitus, identifying distinct suppressive, transformation, and higher-order modulatory roles. These findings highlight the potential of LLMs to investigate maladaptive neural changes underlying tinnitus. This framework may provide the foundation for constructing patient-specific digital twins.

title: Data Provenance and Ethics in the Curricula of U.S. Health AI Education Programs
desc: Failures of deployed clinical artificial intelligence (AI) systems have often originated in how their training data were generated. Whether the programs that train the health AI workforce teach practitioners to examine data provenance is unknown. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of the publicly advertised curricula of health AI education programs at U.S. universities, identified through a structured multisource web search between April and July 2026. Two investigators coded coverage of data provenance (structural, dataset limitations, or data management only), ethics, and sustainability; collaborative structure; technical prerequisites; and the disciplinary background and gender of named instructors. The primary outcome was provenance coverage at the structural or dataset-limitations level. Of 43 candidate entries, 36 programs at 25 institutional units in 21 universities were included. Ethics was covered by 29 programs (80.6%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 65.0 to 90.2), data provenance by 8 (22.2%; 95% CI, 11.7 to 38.1), and structural provenance by 6 (16.7%; 95% CI, 7.9 to 31.9). None of the seven master's degree programs met the primary outcome, and no program addressed sustainability. Eighteen programs included team-based work, but only 5 assembled teams across clinical and technical backgrounds. Of 92 named instructors, 76.1% came from computational disciplines and 3.3% from the social sciences or humanities; among the 51 whose gender could be determined, 66.7% were men. U.S. health AI education programs widely taught ethics but rarely taught how clinical data are produced. None addressed the environmental cost of computation, and most instructors came from computational disciplines.

title: Digital System Physiology: Integrating Mechanistic Models, Artificial Intelligence, and Digital Twins.
desc: [Annual review of physiology] A measurement tells us something about physiology only when a model interprets it, and only when that model keeps the features that matter: organization across scales, feedback, adaptation, and coupling between organs. We use the term digital system physiology for a current version of systems physiology that links many kinds of measurement, mechanistic computation, and artificial intelligence with a clear method for reasoning from data to conclusions and a preset rule for updating. Cardiac electrophysiology is the most developed clinical example. Cardiorenal, metabolic, pulmonary, and neural models are useful but less mature. In all of these areas, the evidence is stronger for mechanistic insight, individualized simulation, and early clinical feasibility than for better patient outcomes. We separate how well a model predicts from how well it explains, and we propose working criteria in which prediction and being built to inform a decision define a twin, with the cadence of updating set by the clinical question rather than by a fixed rule. Progress from here will depend on tracking each patient's state over time, coupling organs together only where it helps, stating uncertainty openly, testing models on data they were not built from, and gathering prospective evidence that matches the intended use.

title: BRIDGE: Learning Brain-Gut Metabolic Evidence for Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis
desc: Alzheimer's disease (AD) diagnosis may benefit from gut metabolic information associated with brain-gut interactions, yet existing models largely analyze cerebral glucose metabolism alone. Although whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) can provide paired brain-gut observations, routine brain examinations rarely include gut imaging, limiting direct use of this information for diagnosis. In this paper, we present BRIDGE (Brain and Gut Representation Integration via Distribution-Guided Enhancement), a two-stage framework for transferring brain-gut metabolic knowledge to brain-only diagnosis. Specifically, BRIDGE integrates a conditional brain-to-gut latent transport module and a disease-evidence-guided cerebral pathway to capture subject-specific cross-organ correspondence and disease-relevant cerebral representations. For the cerebral pathway, a large language model (LLM) helps organize literature-derived descriptors into human-approved semantic anchors that guide feature learning. Additionally, we introduce a counterfactual-guided residual fusion mechanism, which uses matched and non-matched virtual-gut evidence to supervise a confidence gate and dynamically regulate the contribution of transported cross-organ information. At inference, BRIDGE exploits complementary gut-related context using brain PET alone, without measured gut PET. Extensive experiments across public and private cohorts demonstrate that BRIDGE outperforms brain-only and cross-organ baselines, achieving AUC gains of 6.0% and 5.2% over its brain-only counterpart for CN/MCI and CN/AD diagnosis, respectively. Notably, its ability to transfer complementary brain-gut metabolic context while preserving brain PET as the sole inference input highlights its potential for clinically practical diagnosis. Our code is available at https://github.com/CUHK-AIM-Group/BRIDGE.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Microbial Colony Analysis: Plate-Reading Challenges, Method Selection, and Validation.
desc: [Microorganisms] Microbial colony analysis is routinely used in clinical microbiology, pharmaceutical quality control, food safety, and environmental monitoring. Colony enumeration remains challenging because real-world plates frequently show crowding, size variation, background debris, and plate-rim interference. Low contrast on membrane or filter media, weak colony boundaries, and ultra-dense or too-numerous-to-count (TNTC) growth further complicate analysis. These conditions increase counting variability and limit rule-based counters. This review examines artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled colony analysis and links recurrent plate-reading challenges to method selection and validation requirements. We examine traditional threshold- and morphology-based pipelines, object detection, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and density- or keypoint-based estimation. Current evidence is stronger for plate-level triage and semi-quantitative interpretation than for direct colony enumeration. However, evidence supporting routine quantitative colony-forming unit (CFU) reporting across laboratories remains limited. Reliable deployment requires methods suited to plate format, organism, imaging conditions, and intended use, with validation in the target workflow.

title: Testimony from Timelines: Evidence-Grounded Significance Testing of Temporal Clinical Hypotheses
desc: Ask a language model whether sales tend to dip after a product recall, or whether one side effect tends to follow another after a vaccine, and it answers in a fluent sentence that reads like a finding, with no test behind it. Assertions about how events unfold across many cases fill the Web, and each is a temporal hypothesis that only a significance test over the right records can settle. The verifier must specify the null, select the test and decide which records bear on the hypothesis, and any of these choices can go wrong while the conclusion still comes out right. Yet benchmarks for language-model data analysis grade only the conclusion, with the relevant data handed over. We study the problem in health, where a wrong verdict is costly, and present STRATA, a benchmark that grades every decision on the way to a verdict: 8,735 hypotheses over the clinical timelines of vaccine adverse-event reports, with gold plans, evidence sets, p-values and verdicts derived under a released codebook and reproduced by a deterministic oracle. We also propose ART (articulate, retrieve, test), a staged paradigm that exposes each decision as an inspectable output. Extensive experiments with five model configurations show that systems fail mostly at choosing which records count, a verdict-evidence gap that accuracy alone conceals. ART closes most of this gap and brings a 31B open model to within 0.01 of the frontier models under the same paradigm; the frontier models succeed once given the codebook.

title: Rethinking Health Care Regulatory Sandboxes Under the European Union AI Act.
desc: [JMIR AI] AI models have enabled substantial advances in health care. Since the entry into force of the European Union (EU) AI Act in 2024, these systems have become subject to a common regulatory framework in the EU intended to harmonize AI governance across all member states. One of the act's distinctive features is that it accommodates existing economic, technological, and regulatory differences among European countries by leaving certain implementation responsibilities to national authorities. This is evident in regulatory sandboxes, supervised environments for developing, testing, and validating AI systems before deployment. In this viewpoint, we provide a policy-oriented analysis of health care regulatory sandboxes under the EU AI Act and propose recommendations for their design. These recommendations address the need to document model compression techniques that may affect the classification of large high-risk systems above the 1025 floating point operations per second threshold, incorporate explainability into AI systems from the design stage, identify and document biases in health care datasets, clarify the treatment of federated learning parameter updates under the General Data Protection Regulation, and strengthen the oversight of AI agents in clinical environments. The implementation timeline makes this discussion particularly timely given the approaching deadline of August 2, 2027, by which all member states must have established at least one national regulatory sandbox.

title: Beyond Ground Truth: A Heuristic Unsupervised Quality Assurance Engine for Diagnosing Calibrational Blindness in Dental Segmentation
desc: In real-world clinical settings, dental X-ray segmentation using deep learning methods suffers from reliability issues. Even when the segmentation quality is bad, deep learning models show high confidence in their predictions (calibrational blindness). Moreover, in real use, doctors do not have ground-truth masks to check their accuracy. To address this problem, we introduce a simple quality-checking engine called HUS-QA with three stages. We train it on the PRAD (Periapical Dental X-ray) dataset to build our SimCLR self-supervised ResNet-18 U-Net model, which generates the segmentation mask and then evaluates its quality. Our HUS-QA checks the segmentation mask quality without a ground-truth mask. Prediction confidence, edge sharpness, shape connectivity, and area-size penalty are the simple indicators considered in this research. Results show that standard confidence methods fail (r = -0.1394, p = 1.7864e-3, ROC AUC = 0.4275). By contrast, our HUS-QA shows a positive correlation with actual Dice scores (r = 0.4647, p = 3.7510e-28) and achieves a strong ROC-AUC of 0.8405. Therefore, HUS-QA serves as a practical tool for clinical quality control.

title: From LC-MS Metabolomic Profiling to AIEnabled Navigation of NPs Chemical Space: Recent Advances and Emerging Directions.
desc: [Chimia] Natural products (NPs) occupy a unique region of chemical space and continue to provide privileged scaffolds for drug discovery, chemical ecology, and biotechnology. However, the exploration of NP diversity remains constrained by the complexity of biological extracts, the low annotation rate of LC-MS features, and the rediscovery of known metabolites. Recent advances in LC-HRMS/MS-based metabolomics, coupled with expanding spectral and structural databases, molecular networking, and in silico annotation methods, have considerably improved the characterization of complex metabolomes and facilitated large-scale exploration of natural chemical space. Simultaneously, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning approaches are enhancing metabolite annotation, chemical classification, and prioritization, while knowledge graph technologies enable the integration of chemical, taxonomic, biological, and ecological information into interoperable, AI-ready frameworks. This mini-review highlights recent developments that support a transition from conventional metabolite annotation towards effective navigation of NP chemical space. We discuss the role of open data resources, computational metabolomics, knowledge-driven data integration, and emerging AI-assisted tools in accelerating NP discovery. We also examine how biotransformation and chemoenzymatic diversification can extend the boundaries of natural chemical space by generating nature-inspired molecules and previously inaccessible scaffolds. Together, these approaches are paving the way towards a more predictive, integrative, and data-driven paradigm for NP research and bioactive compound discovery.

title: InfantNet: A Large Scale Dataset for Infant Body Pose and Shape Estimation
desc: Infant pose and shape estimation is essential for applications in childcare, developmental monitoring, and medical diagnosis. However, existing methods and datasets are largely designed for adults, and direct transfer to infants fails due to substantial differences in body proportions, articulation limits, and frequent self-occlusion. To address this gap, we introduce InfantNet, the largest real-image infant dataset to date, comprising 108,902 RGB images of infants aged 6-18 months. Each image is annotated with 2D keypoints, and a curated subset of 11,642 images additionally includes 3D pose and shape annotations with full SMIL parameters, verified through multi-view rendering and reprojection-error filtering. We use an iterative annotation pipeline to ensure high fidelity across both 2D and 3D labels. InfantNet establishes a large-scale, comprehensive benchmark for infant 2D keypoint detection and 3D pose-and-shape recovery. Baseline experiments demonstrate that state-of-the-art adult pose estimators do not generalize well to infants, whereas fine-tuning on InfantNet yields a consistent improvement. The gains are even more pronounced for 3D pose and shape estimation, where SMIL-based estimation demonstrates robust performance with accuracy comparable to results reported for SMPL-based models. By releasing the InfantNet dataset and benchmark, we provide a vital resource for advancing infant pose analysis and related healthcare applications.

title: Deep learning predicts IDH1 mutation status in acute myeloid leukemia from bone marrow smears.
desc: [NPJ precision oncology] Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with IDH1 mutations is amenable to targeted therapy, highlighting the need for reliable identification. We developed an attention-based multiple-instance learning model to predict IDH1 mutation status using bone marrow smear whole-slide images from 436 AML patients across four centers in Germany and the US, achieving a mean single pooled ROC-AUC of 0.81. In top tile analysis, model predictions for IDH1 were associated with immature leukemia phenotypes.

title: NECA: Neighbor Event Curve Augmentation for Multi-Horizon ICU Deterioration Prediction
desc: Early prediction of ICU organ dysfunction events supports timely clinical monitoring and intervention, but estimating short-term organ-specific risk from early ICU records remains challenging due to irregular measurements, heterogeneous clinical variables, and the need to predict risk across multiple future horizons. Existing supervised models usually treat each patient as an isolated sample and do not explicitly use the observed event timing of similar historical patients. We propose Neighbor Event-Curve Augmentation (NECA), a model-agnostic method that retrieves training-set patients with similar early-window profiles and converts their subsequent organ dysfunction event onset times into cumulative event-curve features over 6h, 12h, 24h, and 42h. These features are concatenated with the original patient representation and used by standard downstream predictors. On PhysioNet 2012 and a 4,000-stay MIMIC-IV subset, NECA improves average PR-AUC and ROC-AUC across four organ dysfunction event tasks and seven supervised learners. The largest gain appears for neurological dysfunction events, where task-level average PR-AUC increases from 0.461 to 0.557 on PhysioNet 2012. Ablations show that clinically meaningful retrieval and horizon-specific neighbor risk drive most of the improvement, while the full cumulative curve adds task-dependent temporal context. These results support similar-patient event timing as a structured temporal risk signal for ICU organ dysfunction event prediction. The source code will be publicly released upon acceptance of this paper.

title: RNA Tertiary Structure Prediction and Analysis Using NuFold and the NuFold Database.
source: PubMed · Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.)
desc: [Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.)] Accurate prediction of RNA tertiary structure is critical for understanding the functions of diverse non-coding RNAs, yet experimental structure determination remains challenging and resource intensive. Inspired by advances in deep learning for protein structure prediction, NuFold was developed as an end-to-end framework that predicts all-atom RNA tertiary structures directly from sequence. NuFold integrates evolutionary information from multiple sequence alignments and predicted secondary structure features to construct 3D coordinates of RNA. To maximize accessibility, NuFold is available as open-source software, supported by a Google Colab notebook for browser-based prediction and NuFold DB, a large-scale repository of precomputed RNA structures. This chapter provides a practical guide to using these resources, enabling researchers to generate and interpret RNA structural models without extensive computational resources, and thereby facilitating structural and functional studies in RNA biology.

title: Fisher Contrastive Learning to Mitigate Feature Suppression: A Case Study in Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia Diagnosis
desc: Self-supervised contrastive learning (SSCL) learns representations by contrasting augmented views of the same sample, but it can exhibit feature suppression, where dominant or easy-to-learn factors suppress other class-relevant signals, degrading the performance of representations, particularly in high-dimensional data with heterogeneous features. We introduce Fisher Contrastive Learning (FCL), which uses a regularized Fisher trace criterion to address feature suppression. FCL learns embeddings by maximizing the discriminative strength of Fisher discriminant functions, producing representations that preserve class-relevant information implied by the augmentation process. We prove that the representations learned by FCL could alleviate the feature suppression effects. We demonstrate FCL on simulated benchmarks designed to induce feature suppression and on a real-world biomedical application, pretraining on large white blood cell microscopy image dataset and transfer learning for diagnosis of acute promyelocytic leukemia in an external cohort. In all experiments, FCL outperforms the self-supervised baselines and yields more robust and discriminative representations.

title: SpaCut: Transcript-Aware Morphology Fusion for Robust Cell Segmentation in Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomics.
desc: [Advanced science (Weinheim, Baden-Wurttemberg, Germany)] Subcellular Spatial Transcriptomics (SST) offers unprecedented opportunities to decipher tissue architecture at subcellular resolution. Consequently, accurate cell segmentation is a fundamental prerequisite for analyzing SST data, as precise transcript assignment is essential for downstream single-cell interpretation. Existing methods often overlook the spatial organization of transcripts, rely on simplified geometric priors, or struggle to coordinate transcript-derived features with morphology-derived spatial guidance. This limitation restricts their adaptability to irregular cell shapes, often leading to transcript misassignment. To address this, we propose SpaCut, a unified deep learning framework designed to effectively integrate transcriptomic feature learning with dynamic morphological guidance. SpaCut comprises a Gene-Wise Attention (GWA) module and a Nuclei-Guided Attentive Fusion (NGAF) module. GWA encodes the high-dimensional transcript map and aggregates features across multiple depths. NGAF uses the encoded transcript features to modulate distance-based nuclear softmasks and refine nucleus-anchored cell boundaries through progressive training. Extensive evaluations across seven datasets from diverse platforms (including Xenium, CosMx, MERSCOPE, and Stereo-seq) demonstrate that SpaCut significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both segmentation accuracy and consistency with single-cell reference data. The source code is available at https://github.com/wenwenmin/SpaCut.

title: Aligning Medical Vision Language Models at the Capability Boundary with Entropy Adaptive Rubric Grounding
desc: Medical diagnostic reasoning requires verifiable links between visual evidence and clinical knowledge, yet current medical vision language models are aligned with objectives that reward the wrong behavior. Uniform supervised fine tuning lets easy cases dominate updates while clinically critical boundary cases saturate prematurely. Sparse rewards based only on final-answer correctness cannot assess anatomical grounding or clinical logic, inviting reward hacking through answer shortcuts. We propose MedCBR, a two-stage alignment framework coupling boundary-aware preference optimization with rubric-grounded reinforcement learning. First, we construct counterfactual boundary preferences at the model's capability frontier using empirical pass rates and preference pairs that share reasoning prefixes but diverge at decisive diagnostic branches. Difficulty Weighted Boundary Preference Optimization (DBPO) concentrates learning on this calibrated boundary region. Second, we distill reusable clinical rubrics from boundary trajectories and activate them according to prediction entropy. Entropy Gated Grounded Policy Optimization (EGPO) rewards answer correctness, anatomical grounding, and reasoning fidelity while suppressing rubric noise on reliable samples. A reference policy anchored to the boundary-aligned model couples population-level boundary priors with instance-level uncertainty, making diagnostic reasoning more accurate and clinically grounded. Experiments on six medical benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong general, specialized, and reinforcement learning baselines, reaching 61.2% average accuracy with the largest gains on challenging differential diagnosis tasks. Ablations show super-additive gains: combining the two stages exceeds the sum of their individual improvements.

title: From Fiber Architecture to Digital Twins: Characterization, Orientation Modeling, and Artificial Intelligence in Short Fiber-Reinforced Polymer Composites.
desc: [Polymers] Short fiber-reinforced polymer composites (SFRPCs) are widely used in lightweight components because they combine low density, good mechanical performance, and high-volume processability. Their local properties, however, are governed by a fiber architecture-fiber length, orientation, dispersion, and defects-that is created during processing and varies within each molded part. This review examines how this architecture can be measured, predicted, and carried into digital representations of the manufacturing process. It covers the mechanisms that form the orientation state during injection molding; two- and three-dimensional characterization, with emphasis on X-ray micro-computed tomography; orientation models from the Jeffery and Folgar-Tucker equations to anisotropic rotary diffusion and slow-kinetics formulations; and multiscale homogenization. Applications of artificial intelligence are then assessed for image segmentation, orientation prediction, micromechanical surrogates, and physics-informed learning. Finally, published Digital Twin implementations for composite and polymer manufacturing are classified by their level of data integration, and a layered architecture for SFRPCs is proposed. Most existing systems are digital models or digital shadows rather than bidirectionally coupled twins. The main obstacles are the scarcity of paired process-microstructure-property datasets, the lack of uncertainty propagation across scales, and the limited transferability of data-driven models.

title: Anatomical Prior-Guided Routing for 3D Lung Tumor Segmentation
desc: Accurate lung tumor segmentation in computed tomography (CT) is essential for treatment planning, response assessment, and quantitative imaging analysis. However, 3D lung tumor segmentation remains challenging because tumors occupy only a small portion of the whole volume and exhibit heterogeneous appearances across anatomical locations. In patch-based training and sliding-window inference for 3D medical image segmentation, location-dependent heterogeneity is further amplified because cropped image patches provide limited global anatomical context, making it difficult for a model to adapt its feature processing according to the anatomical region from which each patch is extracted. To address this limitation, we propose an Anatomical Prior-guided Routing Module (APRM) for lung tumor segmentation. For each image patch, we obtain anatomical prior information of regional occupancy and deterministically select an anatomical routing gate. The selected gate then performs sparse feature routing over a shared expert adapter pool, enabling anatomy-specific feature adaptation while sharing expert capacity across regions. We evaluate APRM on two datasets with various backbone networks and demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline models. Furthermore, feature visualizations show that APRM produces different feature responses depending on patch location, indicating that the proposed routing mechanism effectively adapts feature processing according to anatomical context.

title: ATP-independent entropy-driven dsRNA unwinding by DDX3X revealed by coarse-grained simulations and deep learning.
desc: [PLoS computational biology] DEAD-box RNA helicases (DDXs) are traditionally known as ATP-dependent motors that unwind double-stranded RNA (dsRNA). Recent experiments, however, show that some DDXs promote dsRNA unwinding even in the absence of ATP, raising a fundamental question about the physical mechanism underlying ATP-independent strand separation. Here, we develop a minimal, physics-based coarse-grained RNA model and incorporate weak, specific interactions between DDX3X and dsRNA, revealing the inherently stochastic nature of unwinding events. The unwinding process must overcome an energy barrier, but thermal fluctuations and entropy gain provide a driving force for RNA remodeling. We identify that dsRNA separation proceeds through rare yet obligatory strand-displacing intermediates facilitated by DDX3X. By combining deep learning-assisted analysis, we further rank the contributions of different entropic components, revealing hydrogen bonding as the dominant factor, followed by base stacking and then the backbone conformation. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized physical mechanism for RNA duplex unwinding and offer an effective framework for studying RNA remodeling kinetics.

title: What Makes Medical Examination Items Difficult? Using Large Language Models to Explore Patterns Associated With Empirical Item Difficulty
desc: Research on medical item difficulty has largely focused on prediction rather than on identifying interpretable patterns associated with empirical difficulty. This study used empirical difficulty labels to guide large language models (LLMs) in inducing difficulty rubrics and examined how rubric guidance affected LLM difficulty judgments. Using training items and their empirical difficulty estimates from the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE) and the Physician Assistant National Certifying Examination (PANCE), Claude Opus 5 induced separate rubrics for absolute and pairwise difficulty judgment. None of the induced rubrics treated surface features, such as stem length, option count, or images, as major sources of difficulty. Several patterns emerged across both examinations, including cue convergence, misleading cues, and option competition, although their specific forms differed. Retrieval of knowledge that could not be derived from the stem was particularly prominent in the PANCE rubrics, whereas the USMLE rubrics placed greater emphasis on integrating multiple clinical cues. We compared commercial and open-weight LLMs on held-out items under unguided and rubric-guided conditions. Rubric guidance changed how models used the difficulty scale but did not consistently improve performance. In absolute judgments, guidance encouraged broader use of the scale and generally improved coarse-grained agreement, without consistently improving rank ordering. In pairwise comparisons, its effects varied across models and examinations, and judgments became more sensitive to presentation order. These findings suggest that the value of label-guided rubric induction may lie more in generating interpretable, testable hypotheses from empirical difficulty data than in reliably improving difficulty judgments.

title: Fractal-Inspired Biorefineries for Sustainable Polymer Production: A Conceptual Framework Integrating Artificial Intelligence and Industry 5.0.
desc: [Polymers] The transition from petroleum-derived polymers to renewable materials requires biorefineries capable of managing the compositional variability and multiscale structure of lignocellulosic biomass. This conceptual narrative review examines fractal-inspired principles-including hierarchical organization, branching, modularity, and finite-range statistical self-similarity-as a design perspective for integrated biorefineries. Deterministic mathematical fractals are distinguished from statistical fractals and hierarchical engineered systems, and methods for characterizing scale-dependent surfaces, porous catalysts, and transport networks are reviewed. The coordinated valorization of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin is then considered within an integrated biomass-to-chemicals framework for producing platform chemicals, functional materials, and polymer precursors. Petroleum crude-to-chemicals processing, including the S-OIL Shaheen Project, is discussed as a limited industrial benchmark for integrated fractionation, residue upgrading, and product diversification rather than as direct evidence of fractal engineering. An integrated framework is proposed in which fractal-inspired design provides the physical and organizational architecture, artificial intelligence supports characterization, prediction, optimization, and control, and Industry 5.0 provides the objectives of sustainability, resilience, and human-centered manufacturing. The framework remains conceptual. Its potential benefits must be evaluated through transport modeling, mass and energy balances, process simulation, experimental comparison, techno-economic analysis, and life-cycle assessment.

title: Does the Citation Matter? Quality, Grounding, and Physician-Rubric Accuracy of Google's AI Overviews for Medical Information
desc: Google's AI Overviews (AIOs) are the first result users encounter when searching the web, shifting the work of selecting and evaluating sources from the user to Gemini. This may be especially consequential for health information, given that Google's traditional algorithm was designed to prioritize quality sources, and inaccurate information carries health risks. We evaluated 3,611 benchmark health questions, comparing each AIO against that question's top five traditional results on source selection and quality. We also evaluated the AIOs' statement grounding in their cited sources and how accurate AIOs were against physician-written rubrics. Overviews appeared for 96.4% of questions but drew on substantially different evidence than traditional search: only 44.4% of the top five results were cited by the corresponding AIO, which instead overrepresented commercial health publishers (e.g., WebMD, Healthline) at the expense of academic and government sources (e.g., Cleveland Clinic, National Health Service). AIO-cited pages scored lower than traditional results on four of six well-established credibility criteria. The grounding of AIO statements to their sources was poor: after correcting for classifier error, an estimated 56.7% of cited statements were supported by their cited page, and a further 20.8% of all statements were factual claims with no citation at all. When AIOs were graded against physicians' rubrics, they earned 38.2% of all available points (e.g., accuracy 54.2%, completeness 21.6%), and among the subset of AIOs whose physician rubric anticipated a specific inaccurate or potentially harmful claim, 22.2% of AIOs contained the harmful content. Notably, the accuracy of AIOs was unrelated to the grounding of their statements. We recommend AIO literacy interventions for users and holding AIOs at least to Google's own health-ranking standards.

title: Local processors: Active dendrites and artificial intelligence.
desc: [Current research in neurobiology] Neuroscience and artificial intelligence have been closely connected for over a century, with each field influencing the other. Modern artificial intelligence systems rely almost exclusively on the point-neuron model, where inputs are linearly summed and passed through a global activation function. Although highly successful, this architecture differs substantially from neural computation that occurs in the brain, and current leading models require massive infrastructure consuming megawatts of power, which contrasts to the brain's remarkable efficiency. One underexplored source of biologically inspired computational principles lies in the dendrites of pyramidal neurons. This review examines the electrical properties of active dendrites and how they could inform the next generation of artificial intelligence architectures. We describe how dendrites can function as semi-independent computational subunits, generating local nonlinear events that implement coincidence detection, signal amplification, and logical operations within a single neuron. We discuss how the structural segregation of different dendritic compartments provides a biologically grounded alternative to global error backpropagation through local credit assignment. We further examine how activity-dependent spine growth and pruning support continual learning without catastrophic forgetting, and how the spatiotemporal selectivity of dendritic integration gives rise to sparse, energy-efficient representations. Together, dendritic computation represents a potential blueprint for artificial intelligence architectures that are adaptive, context-aware, and energetically frugal.

title: When Should AI Decide, Defer, and Deviate? Responsible Automation for Deceased Donor Kidney Allocation
desc: We ask when an AI trained on historical decisions should be allowed to recommend decisions, defer to human experts, or in other cases, flag concerning patterns in data and deviate from past practice. This can be challenging because past decisions record what was done rather than what should have been done, and where data is sparse, a model's predictions may be too uncertain to act on. We provide a framework for addressing this problem using a case study in deceased-donor kidney allocation. Nearly 30% of kidneys recovered from deceased donors in the United States are never transplanted, largely because they are hard to place through the standard waitlist sequence. One can use AI to flag kidneys at risk of delayed or failed placement for out-of-sequence (OOS) allocation, but this comes at the cost of bypassing candidates higher on the waitlist. Thus, OOS allocation should only be used when the organ is demonstrably at high risk of discard on the standard sequence. Using Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network match-run data from 2016-2019 and 2023-2025 (excluding COVID-19-disrupted years), we build the Arbitrator framework, which combines various interpretable models and acts only when the uncertainty in their predictions cannot change the preferred action. Our Arbitrator resolves 93.5% of organ placement decisions using explicit medical criteria learned from data, and defers the remaining 6.5% to a human or a more complex model. We show that the Arbitrator correctly identifies 70.1% of historically discarded low-KDPI kidneys as OOS candidates, projecting that up to 43.9% of historically discarded kidneys could be flagged for expedited placement and potentially transplanted. We then exploit the interpretability of the Arbitrator to create an agentic audit comparing the learned rules to published clinical literature in order to flag decision-making patterns that are contentious.

title: Guidance-Coupled Nullspace Drifting for One-Step Medical Image Reconstruction
desc: Generative reconstruction can recover high-quality images from undersampled acquisitions, but state-of-the-art generative priors commonly rely on iterative sampling. Reducing the number of iterations lowers inference cost but also removes opportunities for progressive distributional refinement, making it difficult to retain image realism without sacrificing reconstruction fidelity. Drift modeling offers an alternative by shifting progressive refinement to training, thereby enabling one-step sampling without an iterative inference trajectory. Existing drifting methods, however, do not account for the imaging operator when modeling distributional drift. We propose DriftRecon, a generative method for one-step medical image reconstruction that performs drifting directly in the nullspace of the imaging operator. DriftRecon uses nullspace-restricted noise to construct training samples and a multiscale generator that incorporates measurement conditioning across resolution levels, with its generated component projected onto the operator nullspace. To control the fidelity--realism trade-off at inference, a conditional guidance parameter continuously steers the same generator between measurement-conditioned and unconditional generation. We derive a guidance-dependent similarity-kernel temperature schedule that preserves the guidance-weighted mass receiving strengthened supervision, thereby progressively localizing drift interactions as guidance increases to limit the associated loss of reconstruction fidelity. Experiments in sparse-view CT and accelerated MRI reconstruction show that DriftRecon outperforms established generative reconstruction methods and recent drifting models while producing reconstructions in a single forward pass.

title: Open-Source Framework for the Visualization, Quantification, and Analysis of 4D Flow and High-Dimensional Magnetic Resonance Images
desc: Background: Four-dimensional (4D) flow cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) captures 3D anatomy and blood velocity across the cardiac cycle, but current post-processing software is closed, varies across platforms, and sits outside open-source image-computing frameworks. We developed an open-source framework for the import, visualization, and quantification of 4D flow and other high-dimensional CMR within SlicerHeart, an extension for 3D Slicer. Methods: Import 4D Flow reads vendor DICOM, applies preprocessing, and stores velocities as a time-resolved vector field; Analyze 4D Flow provides measurement planes, streamline and Doppler-like visualization, segmentation propagation, and quantification. Underlying both, we extended the Insight Toolkit to store five- and higher-dimensional arrays. Flow quantification was compared with a commercial package (cvi42) and 2D phase contrast in 13 patients with congenital heart disease across 108 paired regions of interest (Bland-Altman analysis and intraclass correlation coefficients, ICCs). Consensus-recommended processing methods were also implemented as an open-source library with an automated test suite of analytic and CFD phantoms and clinical acquisitions. Results: The modules integrate with 3D Slicer's segmentation, registration, and rendering tools and export velocity fields and geometry for computational modeling. Agreement with cvi42 was close: forward volume bias -0.1 mL (95% limits of agreement 2.2 to -2.3; ICC 0.997), effective volume per minute bias -0.015 L/min (0.21 to -0.24; ICC 0.994). Against 2D phase contrast, forward volume bias (-2.2 mL) and mean absolute percentage error (21.8%) matched cvi42 (-2.1 mL; 21.3%). Conclusions: This open, extensible framework brings 4D flow CMR into an established image-computing ecosystem and agrees closely with a commercial reference; every step can be inspected, reproduced, and improved.

title: RADIOlogy: A Single-Pass Approach to Training-Free Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection
desc: Current zero-shot anomaly detection methods often rely on complex prompt-learning techniques or computationally expensive sliding-window strategies to achieve fine-grained visual alignment to detect small-scale anomalies. This reliance stems from the fundamental limitation of standard CLIP architectures, where [CLS] token attention and spatial patch pooling struggle to capture subtle, localized anomaly features. While prompt-learning approaches aim to bridge this gap, they typically require a large number of ground-truth segmentation masks from auxiliary datasets, which are often unavailable in specialized domains. In this work, we show an emerging property of multi-head attention pooling in vision-language models: remarkable zero-shot anomaly localization and detection right out of the box. We translate this property into a single-pass anomaly detection technique, RADIOlogy, that does not require dense, windowed execution and significantly outperforms other training-free baselines. Instead, the method relies on a simple contrastive scoring approach that compares the average similarity between vision features and a suite of normal and abnormal prompts. Furthermore, we leverage the agglomerative features of RADIO models to enhance pixel-level anomaly segmentation using a dense anomaly refinement pipeline. Finally, we show how the vision-language family of training-free zero-shot anomaly detection techniques can be applied successfully to the medical domain with minimal modifications. Code is available at https://github.com/jacomof/RADIOlogy.

title: Rural Readiness: Domain Generalization with Adversarially Chosen Domains
desc: Predictive models trained at well-resourced data-rich institutions often fail when deployed in new populations. Motivated by the goal of building clinical diagnosis and decision-making algorithms for data-scarce rural populations using the general knowledge learned from data-rich hospitals, we formulate the fundamental question of \emph{domain generalization with adversarially chosen domains}, which asks a learner to perform on any unseen target domain nearly as well as the worst hypothesis consistent with the evidence from the observed source domains. Assuming only that the hypothesis class contains a "universal" predictor with small error on all $k$ source domains, we characterize the sample complexity of this objective up to logarithmic factors. Letting $d$ denote the VC dimension of the hypothesis class, we find, somewhat surprisingly, that the sample complexity reduces significantly from $Ω(dk)$ to $O(d)$ under a small relaxation of the learning goal in which, roughly speaking, we allow the learned model to compete with hypotheses that perform well on 99% instead of 100% of the source domains. By applying this insight to the meta-distributional setting, in which source domains are selected according to a distribution on distributions, we obtain a corresponding improvement over known sample complexity upper bounds. We also study the effect of data access to the target domain and show that a small labeled sample from the target domain does not improve the worst-case sample complexity on the source domains.

title: D-MOD: Diffusion mode estimation for accelerated MRI
desc: Diffusion models are powerful priors for accelerated MRI reconstruction, but most current methods are posterior samplers, which return a random draw from the posterior. A reproducible and high-quality reconstruction often requires averaging many samples, resulting in a high computational cost. We introduce D-MOD, a fast algorithm that instead provides a posterior mode. It uses a minorize-maximize algorithm on a lower bound of the smoothed log-posterior, which provably increases the objective. Each iteration draws S noisy samples of the current estimate at the current noise level, denoises them with a pretrained diffusion model, and combines their average with the measured k-space through a conjugate-gradient (CG) solve. We anneal the noise levels, as the distance between the bound and its target decays quadratically with noise. On fastMRI brain (T1, T2, FLAIR), a single D-MOD reconstruction exceeds, in PSNR, the 10-sample finite-MMSE estimates of DPS, DAPS and SNORE-P and stays within 0.31 dB of the strongest baselines (DiffPIR, DDS). This approach thus provides a fast deterministic reconstruction algorithm (11-73 times faster than MMSE estimates), which is useful in a clinical setting.

title: EPC-RawDC: Equivariant Physics Constrained 3D Diffusion with Raw Data Consistency for CBCT to CT Image Synthesis
desc: Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) is widely used for image guided and adaptive radiotherapy, but scatter, noise, reconstruction artifacts, and inaccurate Hounsfield units limit its quantitative use. Recent diffusion approaches for CBCT to CT synthesis remain largely image driven, with limited use of the underlying acquisition physics. We propose EPC-RawDC, a conditional 3D latent diffusion framework that combines volumetric generative modeling with two complementary constraints derived from the same scanner specific CBCT forward model. First, geometry equivariant projection constraint exploits the rotational equivariance of the CBCT forward operator by supervising the synthesized CT through correspondingly transformed reference projections. Second, raw data consistency uses noisy projection measurements of the individual acquisition as scan specific supervision during training. The framework was evaluated on two independent clinical cohorts with distinct scanner geometries and projection sources. For JUST, the physics constraints used measured clinical raw CBCT projections acquired with an Elekta system, whereas for SynthRAD2025 the projection data were simulated from the reference CT using a Varian geometry with Poisson photon statistics. EPC-RawDC achieved an SSIM of 0.97 in both cohorts and improved PSNR over DDPM by 2.66 dB on SynthRAD2025 and 2.10 dB on JUST, while reducing mean MAE by 20.3% and 19.0%, respectively. On SynthRAD2025, projection consistency and equivariant errors were reduced by 55.0% and 41.4% relative to DDPM. These results demonstrate that combining a volumetric diffusion prior with scanner geometry and scan specific projection measurements improves quantitative CBCT to CT synthesis across both simulated and measured projection domains. Code available after publication at https://github.com/ALZAHRAALTALIB/EPC-RawDC.

title: Tabular foundation models are not a shortcut to calibrated clinical risk prediction: a pre-registered simulation against the true risk
desc: Tabular foundation models are pretrained networks that predict risk from a table without fitting a model. Whether their risks are correct (calibrated) has been judged on real data, where true risk is unknown. In a pre-registered simulation with known true risks, we compared TabPFN-3.5, TabICLv2 and Mitra-v2 with Firth logistic regression with intercept correction (FLIC) in 58 scenarios and 1,000 random designs, then on four clinical data sets. Foundation models were not a shortcut to calibration. Their calibration slope matched FLIC's within the pre-registered margin in 36 or 37 of 48 core scenarios and was better only at n = 200 with a 3% event rate. Even 3,000 patients were often not enough: with FLIC, TabPFN-3.5 or Mitra-v2, 63%-83% of samples gave risks close to the truth in average, intercept and slope at event rates of 10% and 30%, and 35%-50% at 3%. TabICLv2 did worse (8%-39% and 1%-3%). Across the random designs, foundation models had a lower true calibration error than FLIC beyond the margin in 25%-38% and a higher one in none, though small losses were predicted at n = 3000. On real data, no model resisted a change in event rate between populations; recalibration on 500 local patients largely repaired it.

title: Learning a Motion Manifold to Constrain Ambiguity in Unsupervised 4D Medical Image Interpolation
desc: Unsupervised 4D medical image interpolation reconstructs intermediate anatomical states from temporally sparse observations without intermediate supervision. Distinct motion fields may attain comparable endpoint agreement while producing different intermediate anatomy, giving rise to motion ambiguity. This ambiguity is difficult to constrain when many independently adjustable motion variables must be estimated from the observed endpoints. We develop a framework that learns a motion manifold to restrict candidate motion fields while retaining sample-specific variation. Cross-Sample Spectral Basis Learning extracts recurring motion structure from endpoint-derived dense estimates and encodes it in a shared spectral basis. Sample-Conditioned Cayley Basis Reorientation uses predicted motion coordinates to rotate the effective motion directions for each endpoint pair without increasing the number of independent coordinates. Their composition defines a nonlinear family of complete velocity fields across endpoint pairs, accommodating anatomical and motion-state differences within a restricted representation. Integrating each predicted field supports bidirectional reconstruction at arbitrary intermediate times. Theoretical analysis establishes sufficient conditions under which endpoint observations distinguish nearby motions within the learned family. Experiments on ACDC and 4D-Lung demonstrate state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods trained without intermediate volumes and competitive results against methods using intermediate supervision.

title: Cross-Encoder Anchor Refinement for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection
desc: Zero-shot anomaly detection aims to transfer anomaly discrimination from auxiliary training domains to unseen categories while localizing subtle defects. A key challenge is to construct discriminative references that combine contextual representations with complementary local evidence. We present Cross-Encoder Anchor Refinement (CEAR), which connects two visual encoding paths for the same image at the anchor stage, before normal and anomalous prototypes are constructed. An independent convolutional encoder pretrained for industrial product recognition builds an image-specific memory shared across selected vision transformer (ViT) layers. Spatial anchors read from ViT patch features query this memory through cross-attention and undergo residual refinement. Image-conditioned normal and anomalous queries then gate anchor aggregation to construct prototypes for anomaly scoring. Across 13 industrial and medical datasets, CEAR achieves the best performance in 57 of 68 evaluations spanning image-level detection and pixel-level localization. Notably, CEAR surpasses all other state-of-the-art methods in 41 of 44 pixel-level comparisons. Across 11 localization datasets, mean gains in pixel-level maximum F1 score and average precision are 4.45 and 3.79 percentage points, respectively. This study shows how cross-encoder interaction at the anchor stage can integrate complementary visual representations for fine-grained anomaly localization across domains.

title: Confidence Filtering in Video-Based Gait Assessment: Measurement Error versus Selection Shift
desc: Video-based gait assessment often keeps only high-confidence pose observations, which can lower measurement error but change the movement assessed. We compared confidence selection with budget-matched random selection in a Parkinson-related cohort (n = 96) and an NF2-related replication cohort (n = 18). In the Parkinson-related cohort, confidence selection produced a small but consistent shift in the observed movement summary (+0.05 SD, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.07), while held-out Mini-BESTest error stayed flat (-0.04 points, -0.13 to 0.05); a policy preserving motion-group proportions reduced the shift, while NF2 showed no shift and its predictor did not beat a constant baseline. Because this shift mixes measurement error with selection shift, we decompose and simulate both on the cohort's window structure. Filtering lowers local error when error depends on confidence, but biases the endpoint once confidence tracks movement more than error. In the Parkinson-related data, confidence was only weakly tied to movement (rho = 0.14). There, filtering is harmless if well-tracked windows are unbiased. If instead systematic error only redistributes within participants, filtering can add up to 0.58 degrees. Unchanged clinical error from such small-cohort predictors therefore cannot show that quality filtering preserves the assessed movement.

title: Annotation-Free Representation Learning for Polyp Retrieval in Colonoscopy Videos
desc: Colonoscopy is inherently comparative: reliable visual assessment of polyps often depends on complementary views acquired under different viewpoints and imaging conditions. Retrieving such views requires polyp tracklet representations, which recent contrastive methods learn from temporal cues but still build from manually annotated bounding boxes. We propose an annotation-free framework that constructs tracklet views directly from raw colonoscopy videos, enabling temporal self-supervised learning on full-procedure videos, including frames without visible polyps. On REAL-Colon, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on tracklet retrieval and re-identification, outperforming both self-supervised and supervised baselines. We then introduce few-shot polyp retrieval, a task closer to clinical use, where a few observations of a target polyp are used to retrieve its remaining tracklets: with only two examples, our method surpasses most competing methods given ten. Finally, we show that a modest number of unlabeled procedures suffices for competitive performance, making on-site model development more practical. Code is available at https://github.com/lparolari/freerep.

title: DOSE: Dominance-Guided Ordinal Severity Estimation from Sparse Relative Annotations
desc: Medical severity estimation commonly relies on absolute grade annotations, which are fundamentally ordinal, yet existing methods often treat the grades as independent categories. Learning-to-rank methods, which can be trained using relative annotations based on severity comparisons of image pairs, can provide continuous severity rankings but cannot directly predict discrete severity grades. We propose Dominance-guided Ordinal Severity Estimation from Sparse Relative Annotations (DOSE), a framework for learning ordinal medical severity from sparse pairwise comparisons without using absolute annotations. DOSE aggregates the observed comparisons through a global comparison graph to estimate a dominance score for each image. Differences between dominance scores set cumulative margins in the embedding space, so that pairs with larger estimated severity differences are separated more strongly, and also generate pseudo-pairs that supervise a scalar severity head alongside the observed comparisons. The learned continuous severity axis is converted into discrete grades via label-free score calibration, with tie-anchored segmentation as the main calibration method. In the experiment, DOSE consistently outperformed pairwise-ranking baselines on ACNE04, IDRiD, and LIMUC under different pair budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/TushirSahu/DOSE
